summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); a verse work in thirty-two chapters: the first sets out the purport of all scripture (Viṣṇu's supremacy, the five differences, the gradation of souls, bhakti as the means); the second the principles of interpretation, including the threefold meaning of the Mahābhārata; the third creation; and the rest retell the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata, including Kṛṣṇa's life, in the light of that purport. It closes with the author naming himself the third form of Vāyu, born when 4,300 years of Kali had passed.

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); the seventh of the ten short treatises (daśa-prakaraṇa); it a thirteen-verse discrimination of realities: independent and dependent; Śrī as eternally free; souls graded in liberation and in bondage; eternal and non-eternal insentient things; and the relation of a thing to its properties (no difference for lasting properties; difference-and-identity for temporary ones). It ends: one who knows all this dependent reality to be always under Hari's control is freed from saṃsāra.

summary: one of the thirty-seven works of Madhva collected as the Sarvamūla ('root of all'); the tenth of the ten short treatises (daśa-prakaraṇa); it Madhva's chief independent treatise, in three chapters: the valid scriptures (sadāgama), their authorless and intrinsically valid character, and their teaching of difference (including the reading 'atat tvam asi'); the Lord's supremacy over the perishable (Brahmā, Śiva and the gods) and the imperishable (Lakṣmī); and Viṣṇu's freedom from all defects, even in his avatāras, and the identity of his qualities with his nature.
